title: Two power feeds, one server
summary: How redundant power keeps a server up when a feed fails.

steps.n: Power supply 1 takes mains power from feed A and shares the load with the second supply.
Power supply 2 takes power from feed B, a separate line from a separate breaker.
The server draws current from both supplies, each carrying about half of the load.
A breaker trips or maintenance cuts feed A, so power supply 1 loses its input.
Power supply 2 now carries the whole load alone and the server keeps running.
The management controller writes a redundancy lost event so operators know one feed is gone.

title: Power cycling a hung server with the BMC
summary: From a dead SSH session to a running server without leaving your desk.

steps.n: The operator tries to log in. The host operating system has hung, so nothing answers.
ipmitool chassis power status goes to the BMC on its own network port, which still works.
The BMC reports that power is on, so the hardware is up but the operating system is stuck.
ipmitool sel list shows recent hardware events, such as memory or temperature alarms.
ipmitool chassis power cycle asks the BMC to cut and restore power to the server.
The BMC switches power off and on and the server boots from its disk again.
SSH works once the operating system is back, and the operator records the cause from the event log.

title: A PXE boot step by step
summary: How a blank server finds and loads its installer from the network.

steps.n: The server has no disk to boot from, so its network card broadcasts a request for an address.
The DHCP server answers with an address, the next-server and the name of the boot file.
The firmware downloads the boot loader, such as grubx64.efi, from the TFTP server.
TFTP sends the loader, which then asks for its configuration file and the kernel.
The loader starts the kernel and ramdisk, which run the installer with an answer file.
The installer partitions the disks, installs packages and reboots into the new system.

title: An unattended install with an answer file
summary: What the installer reads so that nobody has to answer questions.

steps.n: The installer downloads a kickstart or autoinstall file from a web server named on the kernel line.
The file describes the disk layout, packages, users and network settings for this class of server.
The installer creates the partitions, filesystems and RAID arrays that the file asks for.
A minimal set of packages is written to disk, and the boot loader is installed.
A first-boot step contacts the configuration tool so the machine gets its specific settings.
Ansible or Puppet applies roles, so the generic install turns into a database or web server.

title: Deploying an image with Ironic
summary: Writing a prepared disk image to a bare metal node.

steps.n: The operator asks for a node with an image and a configuration drive, as if creating a cloud server.
Ironic uses the node BMC to set network boot and power the machine on.
The node boots a small agent image from the network that waits for instructions.
The agent pulls the requested disk image from the image store and writes it to the disk.
Ironic changes the boot device to disk and reboots the node.
cloud-init applies the keys and hostname, and the operator logs in to a running server.

title: A RAID 1 rebuild
summary: From a failed disk to a healthy mirror.

steps.n: mdadm drops the failing disk from the array, which becomes degraded but keeps serving data.
Monitoring alerts on a degraded array so someone acts before a second disk fails.
The operator checks the disk with smartctl and sees failed health and reallocated sectors.
mdadm removes the failed device from the array, and the disk is pulled from the bay.
The replacement is inserted and added to the array with mdadm --add.
mdadm copies every block from the surviving disk to the new one while the array stays online.
The state returns to clean and the operator closes the alert with a note in the inventory.

title: Reading a SMART warning
summary: How a disk reports its own decline before it fails.

steps.n: The disk finds sectors it cannot read and remaps some to its spare area.
The smartd service reads the SMART attributes every half hour and compares them with thresholds.
The count of reallocated sectors rises across several polls, so smartd sends a warning.
Monitoring turns the warning into a ticket for the datacentre team with the serial number.
The operator runs smartctl -a and sees pending sectors as well, a sign of a dying disk.
The disk is replaced in a planned window, long before it takes the array down.

title: How an LACP bond forms
summary: Two cables become one logical link.

steps.n: The server sends LACP messages on each link saying that it wants to form an aggregate.
The second interface does the same toward its own switch port.
Both switch ports are in one port channel and reply with matching keys.
The server sees the same partner key on both links and groups them into one bond.
Each flow is assigned to one link by a hash of addresses and ports, which keeps packets in order.
With many connections, the load spreads across both links.

title: A packet across a leaf-spine fabric
summary: Three hops between racks.

steps.n: Server A sends its packet to the leaf switch at the top of its rack.
The leaf has equal-cost routes to every spine and picks one by hashing the flow.
The spine knows which leaf holds the destination subnet and sends the packet there.
Leaf 2 delivers the packet to server B in its rack.
The return path can take a different spine, which spreads load evenly.
Adding a spine adds a new path for every flow without changing any server.

title: Replacing a failing DIMM
summary: The routine for one sick server.

steps.n: Monitoring shows repeated correctable ECC errors from one memory slot.
The operator cordons the server so workloads move to other machines first.
ipmitool sel elist confirms the same DIMM slot in every event and the operator notes it.
The vendor ships a replacement under warranty, or a spare is taken from on-site stock.
The DIMM is replaced and a memory test runs for a short period to prove the fix.
The host is uncordoned and the repair is recorded against its asset tag.

title: Failure and recovery: a rack loses both feeds
summary: Why redundancy failed and how it was restored.

steps.n: A breaker trips on feed A, as the design allows for.
Feed B alone now carries every server, but the load is above its rated capacity.
The breaker on feed B opens because the rack draws more than one feed can supply.
Monitoring shows servers lost at the same moment, with BMC events for lost power.
On-call confirms that both feeds are down and asks facilities to reset the breakers.
Facilities reset the breakers and the servers boot, but the rack is still overloaded.
The team moves servers out of the rack until one feed can carry the whole load, and adds a power budget to the capacity plan.

title: Failure and recovery: nodes in service reinstall themselves
summary: Why a reboot wiped running servers.

steps.n: The operator updates the provisioning stack and its DHCP configuration changes.
The new configuration offers a boot file to every machine, not only machines marked for build.
A routine kernel update reboots a running node, which has network boot first in its boot order.
The PXE server sends the installer, which repartitions and wipes the disks.
Monitoring shows nodes disappearing and returning as empty machines.
The operator stops the DHCP service and sets the boot order to disk first through the BMC.
Affected nodes are rebuilt from images, and the PXE server now answers only nodes marked as build in inventory.

title: A packet from one pod to another
summary: The path on a Kubernetes cluster with a CNI.

steps.n: Pod A sends the packet out of its virtual ethernet pair into the network namespace of node 1.
Node 1 looks up the destination pod address and finds that it belongs to a pod range on node 2.
The CNI forwards the packet to node 2, either routed directly or wrapped in a VXLAN tunnel.
Node 2 receives the packet, unwraps it if needed and finds the local route to pod B.
The packet enters pod B through its veth pair with the original source address intact.
Pod B answers and the same steps run in reverse, with no NAT in between.

title: From a Service name to a pod
summary: DNS, ClusterIP and kube-proxy working together.

steps.n: The client asks CoreDNS for web.shop.svc.cluster.local.
CoreDNS answers with the Service ClusterIP, a virtual address that no machine owns.
The client opens a connection and the node rules match the destination address.
The rules choose one ready endpoint at random and rewrite the destination to the pod address.
The connection goes to pod 1. Later connections may go to pod 2.
The reply is rewritten back so the client believes it talked to the ClusterIP.

title: A request through an Ingress
summary: Traffic from the internet to a pod.

steps.n: The browser sends an HTTPS request to the public address of the load balancer.
The load balancer passes the connection to one ingress controller pod running on a node.
The controller finishes TLS and matches the host and path against the Ingress rules.
It sends the request to the Service named in the rule, using its endpoints directly.
One ready pod receives the request and builds the response.
The answer goes back along the same path to the browser.

title: How a network policy decides
summary: What the CNI checks for each new connection.

steps.n: The client pod sends a SYN packet toward the server pod.
The datapath finds the labels of the source pod and the destination pod.
The policy engine checks whether any rule allows this source, port and protocol.
If a rule matches, the packet is delivered and the connection is tracked.
If no rule matches and the destination has a default deny, the packet is silently dropped.
Because the packet is dropped, the client sees a timeout and not a refusal.

title: How a sidecar gets injected
summary: Labelling a namespace and creating a pod.

steps.n: The operator sets istio-injection=enabled on the namespace.
A deployment creates a new pod, because existing pods are never changed.
The API server sends the pod definition to the mutating admission webhook of the mesh.
The webhook adds an init container to redirect traffic and the istio-proxy sidecar container.
The pod starts with the app and the proxy, and shows 2/2 ready.
The proxy connects to the control plane and gets its listeners, routes and certificates.

title: A mutual TLS handshake between sidecars
summary: Identity on both sides of one call.

steps.n: istiod gave each proxy a short-lived certificate tied to its service account.
App A sends an ordinary HTTP request. The traffic is redirected to its own proxy.
Proxy A opens a TLS connection to proxy B and presents its certificate.
Proxy B presents its certificate, and both sides check the other against the mesh root.
Proxy B decrypts the request and passes it to app B on localhost, with the caller identity attached.
The reply travels back through both proxies and is encrypted on the wire.

title: A canary release with weights
summary: Sending ten percent of traffic to version 2.

steps.n: The client calls the reviews service. Its proxy intercepts the request.
The proxy consults the route rules it received for the host reviews.
The rule says ninety percent to subset v1 and ten percent to subset v2.
Nine out of ten requests are sent to pods labelled version v1.
One in ten requests reaches version 2, where errors and latency are watched.
If metrics stay healthy, the operator edits the weights step by step until v2 takes all traffic.

title: Timeouts and retries on one call
summary: What the proxy does when a backend is slow.

steps.n: The proxy sets an overall timeout of two seconds for the request.
The first try goes to backend 1 with a per-try timeout of 500 milliseconds.
The per-try timeout passes without a reply, so the proxy gives up on this attempt.
A retry is sent to backend 2, a different endpoint, with a short random delay.
Backend 2 replies in time and the proxy returns the response.
The client only sees a slightly slower success and never knew of the failed attempt.

title: Outlier detection ejects a bad pod
summary: Circuit breaking at the endpoint level.

steps.n: The proxy sends requests round-robin to three healthy pods.
Pod 1 returns server errors on several consecutive requests.
After five consecutive 5xx errors the proxy marks pod 1 as an outlier.
Pod 1 is removed from the pool for thirty seconds, and no new requests are sent to it.
Pods 2 and 3 handle all traffic, so users no longer see the errors.
After the ejection time the pod is tried again. If it fails it is ejected for longer.

title: How configuration reaches the proxies
summary: From kubectl apply to an updated route.

steps.n: The operator applies a routing rule, and the API server stores it.
The control plane notices the change through its watch on the API server.
istiod translates the rule into Envoy listeners, routes, clusters and endpoints.
It sends the new configuration to every affected proxy over a long-lived gRPC stream.
The proxy accepts or rejects the update and tells istiod.
istioctl proxy-status shows SYNCED when the proxy has acknowledged the latest version.

title: Failure and recovery: STRICT mTLS breaks a caller
summary: A plain text client meets a strict destination.

steps.n: The platform team applies a PeerAuthentication in strict mode for the shop namespace.
The web pod has no sidecar, because it started before injection was enabled, so it calls in plain text.
The reviews proxy requires mTLS and resets the connection before any request is read.
Monitoring shows a spike in 503 errors on the storefront with response flag UF.
On-call reads the proxy log, sees UF, and finds the recent PeerAuthentication change.
The mode is set back to permissive, which accepts both kinds of traffic, and errors stop.
The web deployment is restarted so it gets a sidecar, then the mode is set to strict again safely.

title: Failure and recovery: a retry storm
summary: How retries turned a slowdown into an outage.

steps.n: A heavy report makes the database answer in seconds instead of milliseconds.
Inventory times out and retries its query three times for each request.
Orders times out on inventory and retries three times, so each request becomes nine queries.
The storefront repeats the pattern and the database sees twenty-seven queries per user request.
The database falls over under the multiplied load, and every service fails.
On-call removes inner retries, sets per-try timeouts and a retry budget, and enables outlier detection.
Once the load drops back to normal, the database recovers and the services return.
